content: H.M., born in 1926 in Connecticut, is a well-known patient with profound memory impairment who has been extensively studied since the late 1950s. His case has been pivotal in advancing our understanding of the relationship between brain function and memory, as well as in the development of cognitive neuropsychology, a field that investigates brain injuries to infer normal psychological processes. H.M. resided in a care facility in Hartford, Connecticut, where he continued to be the subject of ongoing research. Audio recordings of his conversations with scientists from the 1990s were released in early 2007. H.M. suffered from intractable epilepsy, which has often been attributed, though not conclusively, to a bicycle accident he experienced at the age of seven. He endured partial seizures for many years, followed by tonic-clonic seizures starting at age sixteen. In 1953, he was referred to Dr. William Scoville, a neurosurgeon at Hartford Hospital, for treatment. Scoville localized H.M.'s epilepsy to his medial temporal lobes (MTLs) and proposed surgical resection of these areas as a treatment. On September 1, 1953, Scoville performed a bilateral resection of H.M.'s medial temporal lobes, removing approximately two-thirds of his hippocampal formation, the parahippocampal gyrus (including complete destruction of the entorhinal cortex), and the amygdala. The remaining 2 cm of hippocampal tissue appeared atrophic and nonfunctional due to the loss of the entorhinal cortex, which serves as the primary sensory input to the hippocampus. Additionally, parts of his anterolateral temporal cortex were also removed. Following the surgery, H.M. developed severe anterograde amnesia. While his short-term memory remained intact, he was unable to form new long-term memories. He also exhibited moderate retrograde amnesia, with an inability to recall most events from the three to four days preceding the surgery and some events up to 11 years prior. This retrograde amnesia was temporally graded, meaning older memories were better preserved than more recent ones. Despite these deficits, H.M. retained the ability to form new procedural memories, such as learning motor skills, even though he could not consciously recall learning them. This dissociation between procedural and declarative memory systems has been a cornerstone in understanding memory processes. H.M.'s case was first reported in a 1957 paper by Scoville and Brenda Milner. Their findings revealed that the medial temporal lobes are critical for the formation of semantic and episodic long-term memories. The surgery, while successful in reducing his seizures to a manageable level, resulted in profound memory impairments. Scoville and Milner described his condition as a complete loss of memory for events together with partial retrograde amnesia for the three years leading up to his operation. They also noted that his early memories, personality, and general intelligence were unaffected. H.M.'s preserved ability to perform tasks requiring short-term memory and procedural memory, but not long-term episodic memory, provided evidence that these memory systems are mediated by distinct brain regions. His inability to form new long-term memories, coupled with his ability to recall older memories, suggested that encoding and retrieval of long-term memory information rely on separate neural systems. Studies of H.M. have also demonstrated that working memory does not depend on the medial temporal lobes, as his performance on short-term memory tasks was comparable to that of control subjects. H.M.'s intact language abilities further indicated that language production, comprehension, and lexical memory are independent of the medial temporal structures. Additionally, his ability to acquire new motor skills, as demonstrated in tasks such as mirror drawing and the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, highlighted the preservation of motor learning despite his declarative memory deficits. Experiments involving repetition priming underscored his capacity to acquire implicit (non-conscious) memories, in contrast to his inability to form new explicit semantic and episodic memories. These findings have been instrumental in distinguishing between declarative and non-declarative memory systems. H.M.'s case has also provided insights into spatial memory and the neural structures involved in memory consolidation. Despite his severe anterograde amnesia, he was able to construct a detailed cognitive map of his residence, which he moved into five years after his surgery. This ability was hypothesized to result from daily navigation within the house, potentially involving spared posterior parahippocampal regions. His performance on picture recognition and famous faces tests, albeit limited, suggested the involvement of spared extrahippocampal sites in semantic and recognition memory. H.M.'s temporally graded retrograde amnesia, where older childhood memories were preserved while more recent ones were impaired, provided evidence that older memories do not rely on the medial temporal lobes, whereas younger long-term memories do. This finding supports the hypothesis that the medial temporal lobes play a critical role in the consolidation of memories, gradually transferring them to cortical regions for long-term storage. Interactions between the medial temporal lobes and lateral cortical regions are thought to facilitate this process by forming direct links between cortical representations of experiences. The study of H.M. has revolutionized our understanding of human memory, leading to the rejection of outdated theories and the development of new models of memory organization and function. His case has provided invaluable evidence for the distinction between different types of memory systems and the neural structures underlying them. H.M.'s contributions to neuroscience and psychology have been profound, shaping our understanding of memory processes and their neural substrates.
